content: Imagine you go to the market and buy a packet of salt and a packet of milk. Both packets proudly say '100% PURE'. You bring them home. Are they really pure? What does 'pure' even mean?

Look at the milk packet. It's white and looks exactly the same everywhere. Now, look closely at some soil from the garden. You can see tiny pebbles, some sand, maybe a leaf. If milk looks the same everywhere, does that mean it is 'pure' in science? What do you think?

content.title: Milk vs Pure Water
content.description: Under a microscope, milk has many different things floating in it (fat, proteins, water). Pure water is only water particles.

content: In science, 'pure' means something is made of only ONE kind of particle. Pure water has only water particles. Pure salt has only salt particles. But milk is actually a MIXTURE of water, fat, and proteins!

definition_preview: A substance that consists of only one type of particle (atoms or molecules).
A material made up of two or more different substances which are mixed but are not combined chemically.

question: Which of the following is considered a 'pure substance' in science?

content: Reflection: Explain to a friend why the 'pure' air we breathe is actually not a pure substance according to science.

Connection: This connects to our previous chapter on matter. We learned that matter is made of particles. Now we are looking at whether those particles are all identical (pure substance) or different types mixed together (mixture). Later, we will see how these mixtures are used in medicines and industries.
Mastery Challenge: Go to your kitchen. Find 3 things that are scientific mixtures and 3 things that are pure substances. (Hint: Look for salt, sugar, tap water, milk, and tea).
Now, let's look at mixtures. When you mix sugar in water, it disappears. When you mix chalk in water, it floats and settles. Why?
What do you think is the difference between the sugar-water mix and the chalk-water mix?

content.title: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
content.description: Sugar in water mixes perfectly evenly. Chalk in water does not.

content: The sugar-water is a HOMOGENEOUS mixture (looks uniform). The chalk-water is a HETEROGENEOUS mixture (does not look uniform).

definition_preview: A solid, liquid or gaseous mixture that has the same proportions of its components throughout any given sample.
A mixture in which the composition is not uniform throughout the mixture.

question: Is a pizza a homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture?
options: Homogeneous, because it looks uniformly delicious.
Heterogeneous, because you can see different toppings in different places.

content: Don't assume all clear liquids are pure substances. Saltwater is clear but it's a homogeneous mixture!
When trying to figure out if a mixture is homogeneous or heterogeneous, ask yourself: 'Can I see different parts?' If yes, it's heterogeneous.
Reflection: Why do you think medicines usually come with a 'shake well before use' label? What kind of mixture are they?
Connection: In physics, understanding these mixtures helps us separate them using techniques like filtration or evaporation, which we will learn next!
Mastery Challenge: Create a heterogeneous mixture using only things from your pencil box (e.g., erasers, sharpeners, paper clips). Then explain why it's heterogeneous.
